houthi-strike-jazan-refinery.headline: Houthis claim second drone strike on Saudi Aramco's Jazan refinery in a week
houthi-strike-jazan-refinery.body_md:
Yemen's Houthi movement said its fighters struck Saudi Aramco's Jazan refinery with drones for a second time in less than a week, an escalation that lands squarely on the doorstep of a defence pact Saudi Arabia signed with Turkey and Pakistan barely six days earlier. The Houthi military spokesman, Brigadier General Yahya Saree, said the strike on Thursday was retaliation for what he called Saudi drone incursions into the airspace of Saada and Hajjah, two Houthi-held provinces near the Yemeni-Saudi border. Saudi authorities had not confirmed the claim by the time this article was filed.

The target matters as much as the timing. Jazan is a 400,000-barrel-a-day refinery on Saudi Arabia's Red Sea coast — a piece of the kingdom's energy infrastructure that had gone untouched by direct Houthi fire for four years until late July. That it has now been hit three times in three weeks, with the two most recent strikes arriving within days of Riyadh, Ankara and Islamabad putting their names to a mutual-defence treaty, is the kind of coincidence that reads like a message.

## A refinery that won't stay online

The pattern began on July 25, when Houthi forces combined ballistic missiles and drones in a coordinated assault on Aramco facilities at Jazan and Yanbu — the first direct hit on Saudi energy infrastructure since 2022. That strike damaged Jazan's Integrated Gasification Combined Cycle complex, which supplies the plant's power, steam and hydrogen, along with part of its tank farm; roughly a tenth of stored fuel at the site was affected. The refinery has been offline since July 27.

Aramco had hoped to restart the plant by August 15. A second drone strike on August 9 — two days after the Mecca signing ceremony — forced that date back to August 30, according to an alert from industry monitor IIR cited by Reuters. Thursday's attack, described by Houthi-aligned Sabaa News Agency as retaliation for "Saudi violations of Yemeni airspace and sovereignty," threatens to push the timeline further still. Each additional week offline removes a meaningful slice of diesel and gasoline supply from a market that customers in East Africa and South Asia lean on, at a moment when Middle East refining capacity is already strained by the aftermath of the Iran war and Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries.

## An alliance's first test

The strikes' proximity to the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement is not incidental to why this story matters beyond Yemen's border. On August 7, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif signed a NATO-style pact in the holy city, declaring that "any armed attack against any one of the three states shall be regarded as an attack against them all." It built on a bilateral Saudi-Pakistan defence agreement from September 2025 and drew Turkey — NATO's second-largest military — into the fold alongside Pakistan's nuclear arsenal and Saudi Arabia's oil wealth. Combined, the three countries field roughly 1.4 million active troops, 3,400 aircraft and more than 340 naval vessels, backed by a combined defence budget near $124bn a year.

![Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, whose country joined Saudi Arabia and Pakistan in the Mecca defence pact](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/ba/Turkish_President_Recep_Tayyip_Erdo%C4%9Fan_in_January_2024_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Turkish_President_Recep_Tayyip_Erdo%C4%9Fan_in_January_2024_%28cropped%29.jpg)

The pact was framed, explicitly, as deterrence against exactly this kind of threat — a message aimed as much at Iran, the Houthis' principal patron, as at any single attacker. Instead, the ink was barely dry before Jazan was hit again, and then again. Nothing in the agreement's text commits its signatories to intervene against sub-state actors like the Houthis, and Riyadh has so far responded with the same toolkit it used before the pact existed: limited strikes on Houthi positions, diplomatic protests, and repair crews. That gap between what the alliance promises in principle and what it delivers against a low-cost drone campaign is precisely the credibility question now hanging over it.

## Markets already pricing the risk

Oil prices had been climbing through the second week of August on a mix of factors — lingering uncertainty over whether the Strait of Hormuz would reopen fully, and Iran's list of conditions for a peace settlement with Washington — with Brent crude touching nearly $89 a barrel on August 12 before easing back toward $87 as demand concerns crept back in. The Jazan strikes are a secondary but real contributor to that risk premium: they demonstrate that Houthi forces can reach a major Saudi refinery repeatedly despite the kingdom's air defences, expanding the list of assets traders have to worry about beyond the Strait of Hormuz chokepoint itself.

![Jazan Province on Saudi Arabia's Red Sea coast, where Aramco's refinery has been repeatedly targeted](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/85/Jizan%2C_Saudi_Arabia_locator_map.png/960px-Jizan%2C_Saudi_Arabia_locator_map.png)

Jazan alone is not large enough to move global crude benchmarks on its own — 400,000 barrels a day is a rounding error against roughly 100 million barrels of daily global consumption. But refined-product markets are tighter and more regional than crude markets, and repeated outages at a single plant compound faster than one-off shocks. Every week Jazan stays down adds pressure to diesel and gasoline cracks already elevated by refinery losses elsewhere in the region.

## What comes next

The immediate marker is August 30, Aramco's latest stated restart date for Jazan — a date that has already slipped once and may slip again if strikes continue. Beyond the refinery itself, the sharper question is whether Riyadh, Ankara and Islamabad translate their new pact into a visible joint response, or whether it remains, for now, a paper commitment tested and found wanting in its first three weeks. Iran's ongoing negotiations with Washington over a wider settlement will also shape whether the Houthis have reason to de-escalate — or further incentive to keep proving that Saudi energy infrastructure remains reachable.

deepseek-api-price-hike.headline: DeepSeek to more than quadruple peak-hour AI API prices from 16 August
deepseek-api-price-hike.body_md:
For eighteen months, the pitch from DeepSeek was blunt: frontier-grade AI, at a fraction of what OpenAI or Anthropic charge. That pitch just got a lot less blunt. From 16:00 UTC on 16 August, the Hangzhou lab will charge developers up to twelve times more to use its V4 models during busy periods — a peak-hour surcharge regime that marks the clearest signal yet that the AI industry's price war is winding down, not escalating.

![DeepSeek logo](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/40/Deepseek-logo-icon.png)

**In one sentence:** DeepSeek is raising peak-hour API prices for its V4 models by up to 1,100% from 16 August, closing the cost gap with Western rivals as it eyes an IPO.

## What's actually changing

DeepSeek is introducing, for the first time, separate peak and off-peak billing on its API. Under the new schedule, output tokens for the lightweight V4-Flash model rise from a flat $0.28 per million to $1.32 per million at peak — a jump of more than 370% — with an off-peak rate of $0.66. The larger V4-Pro model goes from $0.87 to $3.96 per million output tokens at peak, more than quadrupling the current price, with off-peak users paying $1.98. Peak hours are defined as 01:00–04:00 and 06:00–10:00 UTC, windows that capture the bulk of both Asian business hours and the US overnight batch-processing crowd. Some token categories rise by over 1,100%, according to a breakdown first reported by Bloomberg and confirmed by Quartz.

DeepSeek framed the move in typically technical language, saying on social media that the new structure would let it "allocate resources more reasonably" and give developers an incentive to shift workloads into quieter windows — a genuine capacity-management argument, given how much compute the off-peak discount is designed to redirect. But the scale of the increase, arriving alongside reports of a fresh capital raise, points to something more than load-balancing.

## Why the cost story matters more than the technology story

DeepSeek's original disruption, in January 2025, wasn't really about benchmark scores — it was about price. The lab trained and served a competitive model for a sliver of what US labs were spending, and it passed that saving on to developers, triggering what some analysts took to calling a "death zone" for costlier, less efficient competitors. Even after this increase, DeepSeek remains cheap by the standards of the field it disrupted: Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.7 charges roughly $5 per million input tokens and $25 per million output tokens, and OpenAI's GPT-5.5 sits close to $5 and $30 respectively. DeepSeek's new peak V4-Pro output rate of $3.96 is still below both.

But the direction of travel is what's notable. A company that built its entire market position on undercutting everyone else is now voluntarily narrowing that gap — not because it has to compete on price anymore, but because, evidently, it no longer wants to. That is a different company than the one that spooked a trillion dollars off US chip stocks in a single week last year.

## The IPO pressure underneath it

DeepSeek is reportedly restarting a funding round targeting close to $8 billion, at a valuation approaching $74 billion (500 billion yuan), with China's national AI investment fund, NetEase, JD.com and IDG Capital among the backers said to be involved, per Bloomberg. The round had reportedly stalled earlier this year after leaked comments from founder Liang Wenfeng unsettled investors; talks are said to have resumed with the aim of closing quietly by late August. Reuters has also reported early-stage preparations for a listing on Shanghai's STAR Market, the exchange board built for high-tech, often loss-making firms.

That backdrop reframes the price increase. A company preparing to sell shares to outside investors — sovereign or otherwise — needs a credible path to margin, not just market share. Serving a near-instant, globally popular API at cut-rate prices is an expensive way to buy growth; DeepSeek's compute bill, like every AI lab's, is dominated by the cost of the underlying chips, most of it running on hardware it cannot legally buy directly from Nvidia due to US export controls. Raising prices even while remaining the cheapest major option available lets DeepSeek improve unit economics without abandoning the underdog positioning that built its user base.

## What it signals for the rest of the field

The practical effect for developers is straightforward: anyone who built cost models around DeepSeek's old flat-rate pricing needs to redo the math, particularly for latency-sensitive applications that can't simply be rescheduled into the off-peak window. The more structural effect is on the narrative around AI infrastructure spending. Part of the bull case for continued heavy capital expenditure by Nvidia's customers has rested on the assumption that inference will keep getting radically cheaper, expanding the addressable market for AI applications. DeepSeek's move doesn't reverse that trend, but it does complicate the assumption that the cheapest possible tier stays cheap indefinitely.

The next marker to watch is whether OpenAI and Anthropic treat this as room to ease their own pricing pressure, or whether they read a maturing DeepSeek as confirmation that the market can support fewer, better-capitalised players at firmer prices. DeepSeek's funding round, if it closes as reported in late August, and any formal STAR Market filing would be the next concrete data points on how serious the shift from growth to profit really is.

twitch-ai-training-backlash.headline: Twitch admits 'nobody would opt in' as it defends default AI training on streams
twitch-ai-training-backlash.body_md:
Twitch has never pretended its streamers are fond of generative AI. Now it has admitted, in public, that they hate it enough to reject it outright — if anyone actually asked them first.

On August 12, the Amazon-owned livestreaming platform rolled out a new privacy setting letting creators stop their broadcasts, archived videos, clips and chat logs from being used to train generative AI models. The catch: the setting is opt-out, not opt-in. Every streamer was automatically enrolled the moment it launched, and disabling it takes a deliberate trip through Settings, then Security and Privacy, then a toggle marked "Training for Generative AI."

Within hours, a post on Twitch's own support forum demanding an opt-in model instead had drawn close to 14,000 upvotes. During a livestream Twitch held to address the anger, chief product officer Mike Minton was asked, plainly, why the company hadn't just made consent the default. He didn't dress it up.

> "If it was opt-in, nobody would opt in. That's honestly the answer."

![Twitch logo](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/26/Twitch_logo.svg)

## An admission, not a defence

It's a rare moment of corporate candour, and it lands badly precisely because it is candid. Minton wasn't claiming streamers were simply unaware of the benefits of AI training, or that a friction-free opt-in flow would surely win people over given time. He was saying the company already knows the answer and chose the setting that overrides it anyway. Mary Kish, Twitch's head of community, added that the opt-out numbers would help the company keep telling itself what it apparently already knows: "our community is not receptive of AI in any form."

What exactly happens to the harvested footage is murkier. Minton told the livestream audience that "Twitch has not been training models," while declining to say what Amazon, the parent company, does with the data once it leaves Twitch's systems. That ambiguity — a subsidiary disclaiming responsibility for what its owner does with the pipe it built — is itself becoming a familiar shape in these disputes. The opt-out also has a gap: it protects a streamer's own broadcasts, but not comments they leave in someone else's chat.

## Why it's more than a UI complaint

Twitch's framing is that this is merely a new setting, not a new practice — implying the data collection was arguably happening already. That's a common move in platform-consent disputes: present the toggle as a gift rather than acknowledge the years without one. Meta and Google have made versions of the same argument, treating anything posted publicly as fair game for training absent an explicit objection.

The reaction suggests that argument no longer buys much goodwill. Streamers make a living from the platform and have limited exit options, which makes the opt-out design feel less like an oversight and more like a bet that inertia will do the enrolling that persuasion couldn't. Twitch's own product chief has now confirmed that bet in his own words.

For Amazon, the reputational cost is a rounding error next to the data value, at least for now. But the pattern — quietly default users into AI training, then defend it by admitting persuasion would fail — is exactly the kind of practice regulators in the UK and EU have been circling on data-consent grounds. Twitch says it will keep the setting as is. The next thing to watch is whether that forum post, and the ones like it, start showing up in a regulator's inbox rather than just the company's.

clop-mass-data-theft-claims.headline: Cl0p hacking group claims mass data theft from Shell, Philips, GE and dozens more
clop-mass-data-theft-claims.body_md:
Nearly 50 companies were named this week on the leak site of Cl0p, one of the world's most prolific ransomware gangs — among them Shell, Philips, General Electric and the payments processor Fiserv. The group says it walked away with tens of gigabytes of internal files: engineering drawings, facility photographs, testing reports, product blueprints. None of the companies has confirmed that any of it is real.

That gap — between a criminal group's public claim and a corporation's ability to say what actually happened — is the story here as much as the breach itself. Cl0p has posted names, file counts and gigabyte figures on its dark-web site. It has not, as of this week, released samples of the data to prove the claims. The named companies, meanwhile, are running forensic reviews that take days or weeks, while their reputations — and in some cases their share prices — sit exposed in the meantime.

## What Cl0p says it has

According to postings reviewed by Reuters, Cl0p claims to have pulled roughly 89 gigabytes of data from Shell, including engineering drawings, photographs of facilities, scans of testing reports and project plans. From Philips, the group claims about 13.5 gigabytes — PDF drawings, diagrams and blueprints. Neither company has verified those figures.

![Shell Centre, the company's headquarters building in London](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/ac/011_Shell_Centre_-_global_headquarters_of_Shell_plc_oil_company_in_London_UK.jpg)

Shell said it was aware of a "possible incident" and is working with security teams to investigate. Philips went further, saying it had "identified and contained an attempted cybersecurity compromise of a specific enterprise server related to internal data," and that the incident does not touch customer-facing systems. Fiserv said that after a "comprehensive review to date" it had found no evidence that customer, banking, transaction or personal data had been compromised, or that its operating environment was affected. GE said it had "initiated our cyber response protocols and are working to assess the potential issue."

Four statements, four different postures — contained, possible, no evidence found, still assessing — which is itself a reasonably accurate snapshot of how little is settled two days after the postings appeared.

## A single vulnerability, dozens of victims

Cl0p's operating model helps explain both the scale of the claim and the difficulty of verifying it. The group doesn't pick targets one at a time. It finds a widely used piece of enterprise software, weaponises a flaw in it, and then scrapes every internet-facing server it can find running that software before anyone patches.

"They don't really target a specific company — they target a specific zero-day vulnerability," said Brandon Parsons of the security firm Ascent Solutions.

This time the software is PTC's Windchill and FlexPLM, product-lifecycle-management tools used by engineering and manufacturing firms to manage design files and testing data — which lines up with the kind of material Cl0p claims to have taken from Shell and Philips. PTC disclosed the underlying flaw, a critical deserialisation bug rated 9.3 out of 10 in severity and now tracked as CVE-2026-12569, in June, along with a fix. Ransom-ISAC, an industry information-sharing group, warned on July 22 that Cl0p affiliates were actively exploiting it. Cl0p began notifying victim companies around July 19 and 20 — meaning some organisations may have had the better part of a month's warning between the patch and the extortion emails.

The pattern is familiar because Cl0p has run it before, at far larger scale. The group sat on a zero-day in Fortra's GoAnywhere file-transfer software before extorting more than 130 organisations in 2023, then a few months later used a separate flaw in Progress Software's MOVEit tool to hit more than 2,600 organisations in a campaign researchers estimate earned it $75 million to $100 million. Before that, it was Accellion's file-transfer appliance. The through-line is always the same: find one popular piece of software, breach as many customers of it as possible, then extort them in bulk from a single leak site.

## The verification problem

What makes this moment uncomfortable for the named companies isn't necessarily that they were breached — plenty of large organisations are, regularly. It's that the public now knows about a claimed breach before the companies themselves can say with confidence what, if anything, was taken. Ransomware leak-site postings are, by design, a pressure tactic: the group wants maximum public attention before it has to prove anything. Some past claims have turned out to involve old data, partial screenshots or exaggerated file counts; others have been entirely accurate. Outsiders — investors among them — have no reliable way to tell which is which until the forensic work is done.

That asymmetry has real consequences. A multinational's operational and reputational risk profile can shift on a leak-site posting alone, before any regulator, auditor or independent investigator has confirmed a thing. If Cl0p's claims hold up, the incident points to a genuine gap in how quickly widely deployed engineering software gets patched across large industrial firms. If they don't, it says something less flattering about how easily a criminal group can put a Fortune 500 name on a leak page and force a market reaction anyway.

## What to watch

The near-term signal will be whether Cl0p actually publishes sample files — its usual next step when a company doesn't pay — which would let outside researchers begin checking the claims against reality. Beyond that, watch whether any of the named companies file breach notifications with regulators, and whether PTC's June patch turns out to have reached its customers before Cl0p's window of exploitation closed. Ransom-ISAC and CISA, which added the Windchill flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on June 25, are both tracking further victims as they surface.

uk-heatwave-ac-bbq-wildfire.headline: UK heatwave drives air-conditioning search boom and calls to ban disposable BBQs
uk-heatwave-ac-bbq-wildfire.body_md:
On the final scorching afternoon of the UK's fifth heatwave of the summer, the property portal Rightmove has a number that says more about where British housing is heading than any temperature reading: searches for homes with air conditioning have risen 104% between May and July compared with the same period last year — effectively doubling.

It is a small, precise signal of a much larger shift. In a Rightmove survey of just over a thousand adults, 87% said a home's ability to stay cool in summer now matters when choosing where to live next; only 11% described their current home as very comfortable in hot weather, while 45% said it struggles to cope at all. Supply has not caught up with that appetite — homes for sale or rent with air conditioning still make up less than 1% of UK listings — which is precisely the kind of scarcity that tends to show up in asking prices once buyers start treating cooling as a baseline feature rather than a luxury import from warmer climates.

![A wall-mounted air conditioning unit fitted to the exterior of a building](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/18/Wall_mount_air_conditioner.jpg)

Friday brought the heatwave's last gasp — up to 33C in the southeast, with thundery breakdowns already moving through Wales and northern England. The Met Office expects a sharper cooldown by the weekend, with London highs falling to around 28C on Saturday and fresher air reaching the southeast by Sunday. But this is the fifth heatwave of the year, not the first, and estates agents report that buyers are no longer pricing homes for the weather they remember — they are pricing them for the weather they now expect every summer.

## Retailers asked to stand down

The same heat has revived a familiar argument about disposable barbecues. England and Wales have recorded 1,017 wildfires so far in 2026, matching the whole of last year's record total, according to the National Fire Chiefs Council. Andy Burnham, who chaired an emergency Cobra meeting on the crisis earlier this month, has renewed his call for retailers to voluntarily pull single-use grills from shelves: "We would say to retailers do not put disposable barbecues on sale at this moment in time."

![A disposable barbecue of the type commonly sold in UK supermarkets](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/cc/Disposable_Barbecue.jpg)

That request leans on a voluntary framework agreed between fire chiefs and the British Retail Consortium back in 2023, under which major chains suspend sales once an extreme heat event is declared imminent — not a statutory ban. Burnham has said ministers will look at a permanent, legally binding restriction during summer months, but for now enforcement rests on retailers choosing to comply, and a public petition for a UK-wide ban stays open for signatures until 15 December.

Both threads point the same direction. Where markets can price climate risk — through a home's listing, its air conditioning, its resale value — they are already doing so, fast and visibly. Where the response depends on public bodies asking companies nicely to change their stock, it moves slower and less certainly. The next test of that gap comes with the weekend cooldown: whether wildfire numbers plateau once the heat breaks, or whether disposable barbecues are still on supermarket shelves the next time a heatwave — the sixth of the year, or the first of 2027 — arrives.

bumble-drops-women-first-rule.headline: Bumble scraps signature 'women-first' chat rule, dividing users
bumble-drops-women-first-rule.body_md:
Bumble spent twelve years selling a single idea: on this dating app, women message first. It was the rule that separated Bumble from Tinder, the pitch that took founder Whitney Wolfe Herd from a Tinder co-founder with a harassment lawsuit behind her to the world's youngest self-made female billionaire when Bumble went public in 2021. On 11 August, the company switched it off. Anyone — man or woman, in a straight match — can now send the first message.

The company frames this as evolution rather than retreat. "Being women-first was never about prescribing just one way to connect," Wolfe Herd said in the announcement. "It was about designing an experience with women's needs in mind." The immediate justification is survey data: Bumble says 66% of women polled would rather men make the first move, and 62% of members felt more confident with greater choice over how a conversation starts. Alongside the change, the company stretched the window to reply to an opener from 24 hours to 72.

![Bumble founder and CEO Whitney Wolfe Herd speaking at TechCrunch Disrupt in 2018](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/3e/TechCrunch_Disrupt_San_Francisco_2018_-_day_2_%2830647055838%29.jpg)

## A brand identity meets a balance sheet

The timing is hard to separate from Bumble's numbers. Second-quarter revenue came in at $210.5 million, down 15.2% year-on-year, and paying users fell 16.4% to roughly 3.2 million — a loss of about 620,000 subscribers in a single year. Full-year 2025 revenue had already dropped nearly 10%, to around $966 million, and the stock has shed close to half its value over the past twelve months. Reuters reported in June that Bumble was working with Morgan Stanley to explore strategic alternatives, though no deal was confirmed. Against that backdrop, the founding rule that once generated headlines and app-store downloads had become, by the company's own account, a friction point: fewer messages sent, fewer conversations started, fewer reasons for women to open the app at all.

Bumble had already been loosening the model. Its 2024 "Opening Moves" feature let women post a question men could answer to break the ice without composing a line from scratch — a soft acknowledgment that the original mechanic asked a lot of users on a bad-dating-app day. Executives have also floated swipe-free formats, in-person events and AI matching tools as they try to arrest what the industry broadly calls swipe fatigue, a problem hitting Match Group's Tinder and Hinge just as hard.

The reaction split roughly along the line Bumble's own data predicted. Some users, especially those citing the mental load of always messaging first, welcomed the change. Others said it erases the one feature that made the app worth choosing over Tinder, and some women flagged a familiar worry: that the 72-hour window and open messaging simply reopen the door to the unsolicited-message problem Bumble was built to close.

Bumble reports full third-quarter results in November, the first window to see whether scrapping its founding rule moves the user and revenue numbers it was designed to fix — or merely confirms that the identity it built the company on had already stopped being the reason people used it.

japan-record-rain-narita-disruption.headline: 'Unprecedented' rain kills four in Japan, strands thousands at Narita airport
japan-record-rain-narita-disruption.body_md:
The rain that fell on Chiba prefecture on Thursday night did not arrive as a storm in any conventional sense — no typhoon eye, no dramatic landfall footage. It came instead as a stalled band of moisture that simply refused to move on, dumping water on the same patch of ground east of Tokyo for hour after hour until the Japan Meteorological Agency ran out of room on its own warning scale.

By the time it eased on Friday morning, four people were dead, one was missing, more than 400,000 residents across Chiba were under evacuation orders, and roughly 7,000 travellers had spent the night camped across the terminal floors of Narita International Airport — Japan's principal gateway to the rest of the world, and for twelve hours or so, an island cut off by water on every side.

## A warning Japan had never issued before

The Meteorological Agency's five-tier rain warning system exists mostly to be talked about in the abstract. Level 5 — the top tier, reserved for conditions in which "lives may be in imminent danger" — had never been declared for Chiba prefecture until 11:40pm local time on Thursday, when the agency issued it for the town of Shirako and then extended it within hours to roughly twenty municipalities, including the prefectural capital, Ichihara, Sakura and Ichikawa.

The numbers behind that decision were stark. Chiba city recorded 348 millimetres of rain in twelve hours — the highest since records began there — and more than 360mm fell across parts of the prefecture in 24 hours, close to three times what the region typically sees across the whole of August. At the peak, rain fell over Chiba's central ward at more than 115mm an hour; near Sakura City, roughly 100mm fell in a single hour before 9pm.

> "This is shaping up to be an unprecedented level of heavy rain," a Japan Meteorological Agency official said, warning that lives were at immediate risk.

One person was found dead in Ichikawa; two others trapped in a submerged car were pulled out alive nearby in Kashiwa. Roughly 45,000 households lost power, roads across the prefecture flooded, and Japan's Self-Defense Forces were sent in to assist search-and-rescue operations alongside local authorities, with one person still unaccounted for as of Friday.

## A night on the terminal floor

The most visible casualty of the storm was Narita itself. Rail, bus and expressway links into the airport were severed Thursday night as floodwater rose over roads and rail platforms, leaving passengers with nowhere to go. Airport staff opened areas normally off-limits to the public, handing out blankets, water, snacks and sleeping bags; footage aired by public broadcaster NHK showed travellers queuing for supplies before bedding down across the concourses of all three terminals. About 1,700 more people sheltered at the Chiba prefectural government building.

![Narita International Airport, Tokyo's principal international gateway](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/03/013_Tokyo_Narita_International_Airport%2C_Japan_-_%E3%83%A6%E3%83%8A%E3%82%A4%E3%83%86%E3%83%83%E3%83%89%E8%88%AA%E7%A9%BA.JPG)

The timing compounded the disruption. The storm hit during Obon, the mid-August holiday week when domestic and international travel through Japan's airports typically peaks. Japan Airlines said some flights would face delays but that cancellations were not currently expected, and airport operators said services were scheduled to resume normally on Friday as surface transport links gradually came back — some trains connecting Narita to central Tokyo had resumed by Friday morning, while highway operator NEXCO East kept sections of expressway closed and traffic backed up onto alternative routes.

## Why a single storm reads as a supply-chain event

Narita is not simply Tokyo's busiest passenger airport. It is Japan's largest air-cargo hub and one of the ten busiest freight airports in the world, handling roughly 2.36 million tonnes of loaded and unloaded cargo a year and around 30,000 international cargo flights — the primary conduit linking Japanese electronics, machinery, pharmaceuticals and automotive parts to markets in North America and Europe. When the roads and rail lines feeding it flood, the disruption is not contained to stranded holidaymakers; it touches the freight schedules that manufacturers and retailers on several continents build their inventory planning around.

That is the pattern climate researchers have been flagging for years now: it is rarely the headline disaster — the typhoon with a name and a forecast track — that does the most economic damage to modern logistics networks. It is the unnamed, slow-moving rain event that a five-tier warning system was never quite calibrated to describe until it had to invent a new use for its top tier. Chiba's flooding did not touch a runway or ground a single scheduled flight through mechanical failure. It simply removed, for the better part of a day, every way of getting to one of Asia's busiest airports — which for a trade-dependent economy amounts to much the same thing.

## What comes next

The immediate priority is the search for the one person still missing and continued relief operations in Chiba's flooded neighbourhoods; the JMA has warned that further downpours remain possible in the coming days as the same moist air mass lingers over eastern Japan. For airlines and shippers, the test is how quickly rail and road access to Narita normalises through the rest of Obon week — and whether insurers and logistics planners treat this as an isolated event or, as record-breaking rainfall becomes a more frequent entry in Japan's weather data, the kind of risk that reroutes contingency planning permanently.

romania-nuclear-plant-drought-shutdown.headline: Romania shuts sole nuclear plant as Danube drought threatens cooling water
romania-nuclear-plant-drought-shutdown.body_md:
Record-low Danube levels forced Romania to take both Cernavoda reactors offline for roughly ten days, a first since 2003, deepening a heatwave-driven power crunch.

Water availability is emerging as a hard constraint on power generation during peak-demand periods—a direct market risk, not just a climate story. The cascade is brutal: heat drives demand up while heat reduces cooling-water availability, forcing shutdown of clean baseload power at exactly the wrong moment, tightening energy markets across Europe.

Key facts:
- Both Cernavoda nuclear reactors went offline due to insufficient cooling water from record-low Danube levels; first total shutdown since 2003
- Reactors remained offline for approximately 10 days during peak summer demand amid a European heatwave
- Romania's nuclear plant is a major baseload power source; its loss deepens regional energy shortages and pressures European power prices

korea-retail-investor-losses.headline: South Korean stock market's wild swings leave retail investors nursing steep losses
korea-retail-investor-losses.body_md:
For months, South Korea's stock market looked like the trade of the decade. The Kospi index roughly doubled between January and June, riding the same AI and semiconductor enthusiasm that lifted Nvidia and its peers, with Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix as the local proxies. Then, in June, it broke. What followed has left ordinary Koreans nursing losses that, for some, wiped out years of savings in a matter of weeks.

![Yeouido, Seoul's financial district, seen from the Han River](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c9/Skyline_of_Yeouido%2C_a_prominent_finance_district_in_Seoul.jpg)

"I got completely swept up in the frenzy," said Kim Han-kyung, a Seoul resident in her late thirties who started trading in May. "Now, I'm honestly scared." She has since set herself two rules, she told local media: never invest in the Korean stock market again, and follow the first rule. Lee Jung-min, 40, took out a 50 million won loan against his apartment to trade — and lost heavily. "The government put fuel into the fire with those leveraged ETFs," he said. "I think it's wrong how they turned the stock market into a casino."

The products he means are single-stock leveraged ETFs tracking Samsung and SK Hynix, launched on 27 May to give retail traders the kind of geared exposure previously available only offshore. Domestic investors poured in 14 trillion won ($9.7bn), seven times what foreigners bought, and came to hold 92 percent of the positions. When chip stocks reversed, the KODEX SK Hynix leveraged fund fell more than 80 percent from its June peak. The Kospi itself dropped from above 8,800 points to 6,820 by 16 July — a decline of more than 25 percent — logging its worst monthly fall since the 2008 financial crisis and tripping circuit-breaker halts 19 times since the ETFs debuted.

## A market built on retail money

The damage was concentrated because Korea's market is unusually retail-driven: individuals accounted for roughly 64 percent of annual trading value, against about 30 percent in the US or Japan. Regulators say margin calls hit 1.2 million accounts — about one in 30 adults — and between 320,000 and 360,000 were forcibly liquidated, wiping out principal entirely for many. Estimated cumulative losses on the leveraged products alone run near $38bn. Late last month, protesters laid roughly 30 funeral wreaths outside the National Assembly, reading "abolish single-stock leveraged ETFs" and "we'll get even with our votes." Finance minister Koo Yun-cheol apologised in parliament: "We sincerely apologise for not thoroughly considering how these products would perform after their launch." Authorities have since raised the minimum deposit for leveraged ETF trading to 30 million won ($21,000) and set up a debt-counselling hotline.

The irony is that the market has since turned again. The Kospi reclaimed the 7,000-point mark on Thursday, up some 22 percent from its 30 July low and back in technical bull territory as chip stocks rallied once more. But the retail money that drove the mania hasn't followed: individuals' share of trading value has slid from 48 percent in January to about 31 percent in July, the sharpest such retreat on record. Whether that caution holds — or whether the next AI-fuelled rally pulls Korean households back in — is the question regulators are now watching closest.
